en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on Vessantara, Concerning the Question on Inference.
11. The Question on the Realization of Nibbāna “Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘Nibbāna is not past, not future, not present; it is not arisen, not unarisen, and not something to be made to arise.’”
“Venerable Nāgasena, here, whoever practices rightly realizes *nibbāna*: does he realize what has already arisen, or does he realize it after having produced it?
“Whosoever, Great King, practices rightly and realizes *nibbāna*, he does not realize what has already arisen, nor does he realize it after having produced it.
Nevertheless, Great King, there exists this element of *nibbāna* (nibbānadhātu) which he who practices rightly realizes.”
“Do not, venerable Nāgasena, explain this question by concealing it; explain it by making it open and clear.
With zeal and enthusiasm, scatter all that you have learned right here!
For in this matter the people are bewildered, filled with doubt, and fallen into uncertainty; break this arrow of the internal defect.”

“There exists, Great King, this element of Nibbāna— peaceful, blissful, and sublime— which one who has entered upon the right practice, contemplating formations according to the Teacher’s instruction,
realizes through wisdom. Just as a pupil, Great King, realizes a craft through wisdom according to the teacher’s instruction, even so, Great King,
one who has entered upon the right practice realizes Nibbāna through wisdom according to the Teacher’s instruction.”
But how, then, is that Nibbāna to be seen?
It is to be seen as free from distress, free from calamity, fearless, secure, peaceful, blissful, sweet, sublime, pure, and cool.

Great King, it is like a man who, being burned by a fire blazing with a great heap of wood and glowing embers, were to escape from it through effort and, entering a place free from fire, find supreme happiness there.
In the same way, Great King, he who practices rightly realizes through wise attention the supreme bliss of Nibbāna, wherein the threefold heat of the fires has been dispelled.
Just as fire, Great King, is to be regarded as the threefold fire;
and just as the person within the fire, so should one who practices rightly be regarded.
Just as a place free from fire is to be seen, so too is Nibbāna to be seen.

Or again, Great King, just as a man who has gone to a heap of refuse containing the corpses of snakes, dogs, humans, and birds, and having entered among the tangled masses of corpses and matted hair, might with effort free himself from there and enter a place free from corpses; [so it is with Nibbāna].
In that case, one would obtain supreme happiness;
even so, Great King, he who practices rightly realizes through systematic attention the supreme happiness of Nibbāna, from which the carrion of the defilements has been removed.
Great King, just as carrion is, so should the five strands of sensual pleasure be regarded.
Just as the man who has gone to the corpse-pit should be regarded, so should one who practices rightly be regarded;
just as the place free from corpses should be regarded, so should Nibbāna be regarded.

Or again, Great King, just as a man—frightened, terrified, trembling, his mind agitated and distraught—might through effort escape from that [pit], enter a firm, stable, immovable place of fearlessness, and there obtain supreme happiness; [so it is with the practitioner].
In the same way, Great King, he who practices rightly realizes through wise attention the supreme bliss of Nibbāna, from which fear and terror have departed.
Just as there is fear, Great King, so should the recurring fear that arises in dependence upon birth, aging, sickness, and death be regarded.
And just as there is the frightened person, so should the one who practices rightly be regarded.
Just as a place of safety is to be regarded, so too is Nibbāna to be seen. Or again, Great King,

just as a man who has fallen into a place of filth, mud, and mire might, through effort, drive away that mud and mire, reach a spot that is perfectly pure and stainless, and there obtain supreme happiness— even so, Great King,
he who practices rightly realizes Nibbāna, the supreme happiness, wherein the mud and mire of the defilements have been removed through wise attention.
Just as, Great King, the *kalala* is to be regarded, so should gain, honor, and fame be regarded;
just as a man who has entered the *kalala* is to be regarded, so should one who practices rightly be regarded;
just as a region that is pure and free from stain is to be regarded, so should Nibbāna be regarded.
And how, Great King, does one who has entered upon the right practice realize that Nibbāna?
One who has entered upon the right practice, Great King, contemplates the process of conditioned formations (*saṅkhārā*).

While contemplating their process, he sees birth therein, he sees aging, he sees sickness, and he sees death; he sees nothing therein as pleasant or agreeable, neither in the beginning, nor in the middle, nor in the end.
Thus, he does not see anything therein that is fit to be grasped.

Great King, just as a man, when looking at an iron ball heated all day, glowing, hot, and solidified, does not see anywhere—whether at the beginning, the middle, or the end—a portion fit to be grasped;
even so, Great King, he who comprehends the occurrence of conditioned phenomena, while comprehending that occurrence, [sees nothing fit to be grasped].
Therein he sees birth, he sees aging, he sees sickness, he sees death;
he does not see therein anything pleasant or agreeable, either in the beginning, in the middle, or in the end.

Therein he sees nothing worth grasping; as he sees nothing worth grasping, dissatisfaction settles in his mind, a burning descends upon his body, and being without protection, without refuge, and having become one who has no refuge, he becomes disenchanted with states of existence.
"Just as, Great King, a man might enter a great mass of blazing fire, and finding therein no protection, no refuge, and having become without refuge, he would grow weary of the fire;

even so, Great King, for one who does not see anything to be grasped, discontent arises in the mind, a burning sensation descends upon the body, and finding no protection, no refuge, and having become without refuge, he grows weary of states of existence (*bhava*).
As he sees danger in the process of becoming, this thought arises in him: 'This process of becoming is indeed heated.'"
"It is burning, blazing, full of suffering, and full of despair. If anyone could find the non-arising [of this],
that would be peace, that would be sublime— namely, the stilling of all formations, the relinquishing of all acquisitions,
the destruction of craving, dispassion, cessation, Nibbāna."
Thus, because of this non-occurrence, his mind leaps forward, becomes serene, exults, and rejoices, thinking: "I have indeed attained the escape.

Great King, it is just as when a man who has lost his way and wandered into a foreign land sees the path leading out and leaps forward upon it, becomes serene, exults, and rejoices, thinking: "I have found the path leading out."

In the same way, Great King, when there is occurrence [of suffering], one who sees danger finds the mind leaping forward, becoming confident, gladdened, and satisfied regarding non-occurrence, thinking: "I have indeed attained the escape.
For the sake of that non-occurrence, he applies himself to the path, seeks it, develops it, and cultivates it repeatedly.
For that purpose, his mindfulness becomes established; for that purpose, his energy becomes established; for that purpose, his rapture becomes established. For him—
"As he attends to that mind again and again, having transcended its occurrence, he enters into its non-occurrence.
Having reached non-occurrence, O Great King, one who practices rightly is said to 'realize Nibbāna.
"Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it."
The eleventh question: On the Realization of Nibbāna.
